Tufting is a type of textile manufacturing in which a thread is inserted on a primary base. It is an ancient technique for making warm garments, especially mittens. After the knitting is done, short U-shaped loops of extra yarn are introduced through the fabric from the outside so that their ends point inwards (e.g., towards the hand inside the mitten).

Usually, the tuft yarns form a regular array of "dots" on the outside, sometimes in a contrasting color (e.g., white on red). On the inside, the tuft yarns may be tied for security, although they need not be. The ends of the tuft yarns are then frayed, so that they will subsequently felt, creating a dense, insulating layer within the knitted garment.

Tufting was first developed by carpet manufacturers in Dalton, Georgia. A tufted piece is completed in three steps: tufting, gluing, then backing and finishing. When tufting, the work is completed from the backside of the finished piece. A loop-pile machine sends yarn through the primary backing and leaves the loops uncut. A cut-pile machine produces plush or shaggy carpet by cutting the yarn as it comes through to the front of the piece. Tufted rugs can be made with colored yarn to create a design, or plain yarn can be tufted and then dyed in a separate process.

A tufting gun is a tool commonly used to automate the tufting process, more specifically in the realm of rug making. The yarn is fed through a hollow needle, that penetrates the stretched cloth backing for a modifiable length.

They can usually create two types of rugs, a cut or loop pile. A cut pile rug's yarn is snipped every other loop into the backing, creating a “U” shape from the side profile, while a loop pile rug isn't snipped and creates a continuous “M” or “W”. Tufting guns are useful tools for both mass production and home use due to its flexibility in scale and color variation.

Materials

Tufting cloth stretched on frame
Tufting requires the use of specialized primary backing fabric, which is often composed of woven polypropylene. Primary backing fabric is produced with a range of densities and weaving styles, allowing for use with different gauges of needles. Primary backing fabric must be stretched tightly to the frame so that it is stable enough to withstand the pressure of the tufting gun and taught enough for the yarn to be held in place. Tufting frames are generally constructed of wood, with carpet tacks or grippers around the edge to hold the primary backing fabric in place. Eye hooks are an important addition to a tufting frame, they are used as yarn feeders and work to keep the tension consistent. The frame must be sturdy and can be either freestanding or clamped to a tabletop. It is important to keep pressure and speed consistent when tufting so that the amount of yarn per square inch of the fabric is consistent.[5] Any mistakes in the design can be corrected throughout the tufting process by simply pulling out yarn strands from the primary backing fabric and re-tufting the area. Designs can drawn directly on to the primary backing fabric, this can be done freehand or with the aid of a projector.

After tufting is completed, the tufted piece requires a coat of latex glue on the back to keep the tufts anchored in their place. Latex glue is beneficial for tufted pieces as it provides flexibility and dimensional stability. The piece should remain stretched on the frame until the glue has finished drying to avoid loss of shape and the possibility of mildew. A secondary backing layer is then applied, providing further dimensional stability and protection for the finished piece as well as improving its appearance. A wide variety of materials can be used for the secondary backing fabric depending on the intended use of the piece. Felt, canvas, drill, and other harder wearing materials can be used for floor rugs, however backing fabric for wall hangings need only be aesthetic, as it is only required to cover up the glue layer and does not need to be hard wearing. • . WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These mica colors come in zipper topped little plastic bags. They have 5 g of colors in them and are an assortment of textures and types. The quality is high on all of their mica colors that I have tried and I have tried quite a few from this company.

DO THESE REALLY HAVE 5G in them?
I weighed out all of the packages of colors from BLACK DIAMOND and I did find that all of them measured 5g with only two exceptions. I did swatches for you all to see, so those two could have been short because of that. Some packages were even a bit over.

COLOR DISCUSSION
I have a large collection of micas so I would like to take a moment to tell you what these are like. If I do not mention texture, then assume it is the typical texture of micas which are fine powders that have pearl appearance to them when mixed.

BLACK DIAMOND
The namesake of the company, this color is made from what I call mini glitter. It is made up of black and silver very tiny specs of glitter. This won't change a color of something, but it will play well with other micas that are finer as a nice accent.

DIAMOND BATTLESHIP GREY
This color is also a bit coarser texture than typical mica powders. This has gunmetal mini glitter with lighter diamond silver specs in it too. Just like BLACK DIAMOND this is more for accent texture than solid color transformations. You will need a LOT of it to get a good color if you do.

LUX BLUE
This is another micro/mini glitter color. It has a denim blue type glitter particle which is great for accents mixed with other colors as background or if you like clear soap or resin and want just suspended particles in it.

BLUE SLATE
This color is typical texture mica. It has a very faded denim color with silver shimmer in it

DIAMOND DEEP BLUE SEA
This is another one of those micro/mini glitter powders. This one is a brilliant blue more on the lines of crayon blue with silver sparkles in it. IT is about halfway between the solid glittery ones and a fine mica powder.

COPPER PENNY
This is a beautiful metallic copper just like a new penny.

DIAMOND LIQUID FIRE
This is simply LIQUID FIRE with some diamond effect added to it. This color is fuchsia with a gorgeous intense violet blue duchrome pearl in it. The white/silver diamond specs dress it up a bit.

DIAMOND GOLD
This is a coppery gold color with diamond effect added. It is halfway between typical mica powders and a solid diamond powder.

GHOST COPPER PEARL
This is one of my HAVE TO HAVE colors. It is a translucent whitish powder with a beautiful pinkish copper duochrome to it. It has a wisp of color to it so that it is not IN YOUR FACE but almost mystical in nature. I love this as a highlighter for coppery looks with red hair.

DIAMOND EFFECT
This is made up of the silver sparkly little bits which are added to many of the other colors for accent that contain the name DIAMOND in them. You can use this alone or add it to any color you like, mixing well.

WHAT DO I DO WITH THESE?
I use micas for a lot of things. These are good for soap, lotions, resin, body oils, shampoos, watercolors, topcoats for nails and walls (in clear bases), and when I am sure of safety I use them as makeup too.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This collection of mica colors is a nice assortment. The bags are filled accurately and the colors are beautiful. If you like that extra zing of diamond sparkle, you might want to check this one out. It is a nice variety to choose from.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS for this collection. It has a lot to choose from and at this price it is only $2 a color which is good. I thought it was high at first, but when I thought about it, I realized it is quite an assortment.

PHOTOS
It is difficult to capture the true color of mica powders as our eyes see them as they are more multi-dimensional than cameras tend to pick up. I have taken these in dimmer light than normal to try to let you see the nuances the colors have. Notice in some photos, the same color can look very different depending on the angle.

These are extra supports which you put on either end of longer pieces of material you are going to engrave. They offer support, but also allow for smooth movement back and forth in conjunction with the roller device so that your long item can be engraved.

POSITION
One thing I have learned in my journey into laser engraving is that you can not be in a hurry. This is not a plug and play craft. This is a craft for patience and persistence to get the results you need. These roller stands have to be placed in just the right position to be useful. I highly suggest you mark the table top somehow once you have them where they work well so that you can put them there for the final product.

TESTING
Do not plan to just slap on a long piece of wood and do your project. Have some scrap wood (or whatever you are working on) handy so that you can test for best placement and results. Once you have it, secure the roller stands or at least mark them well with painters tape and the do your final project.

FLAT WOOD
I can not stress this enough. Using this type of process means you will not have clips handy to secure wood that is at all warped. Warped wood leads to distorted images. In this case, it won't work right with the roller and roller stands if it is not flat. Be sure to check for that BEFORE you try to start your project.
